text.p: European Union fisheries ministers on Tuesday agreed by majority vote a programme to reduce fishing by up to 30 percent over five years to the end of 2001 in a bid to save endangered stocks, EU officials said.
Britain, which had insisted that the problem of Spanish and Dutch "quota hoppers" be tackled first, voted against -- as did France, which had called for a 15 percent reduction over three years.

"We are not prepared to continue to see a situation where over a quarter of the British fishing fleet is foreign owned and foreign controlled," British Fisheries Minister Tony Baldry told reporters after the vote.

Fisheries is one of the few areas where the EU sets national quotas, he noted, stressing "U.K. fish must be for U.K. fishermen." "The U.K. can well meet that (30 percent) target by eliminating quota hoppers from our register and that we are determined to do," he added.

Baldry reiterated that Britain would not allow a ministerial review of the EU Treaty, the inter-governmental conference (IGC), to conclude until this issue of crucial importance to Britain was resolved.
Baldry, whose Conservative party is fighting for fishermen's votes in elections on May 1, attacked the fisheries policy of the opposition Labour party.

"The leader of the oppostion Tony Blair has been using some very weasel words on what, if there were to be a Labour government, they might or might not do at the IGC," he said, urging the Labour Party to pledge to block the IGC until the quota hoppers problem was resolved.

EU officials said that Tuesday's deal, which was reached after Swedish concern over a Baltic cod fishing cutback was resolved, would free up hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to restructure Europe's fishing industry.

The European Commission originally proposed a 40 percent reduction over six years but this was fiercely rejected by EU member states, fearful of the political backlash if poor fishing communities were thrown out of work.
EU governments won greater flexibility in choosing whether to cut fish catches by laying up vessels, or by reducing fishing time at sea -- or a combination of both.
Stocks which are overfished, rather than endangered, are subject to a 20 percent reduction by the end of 2001.

Small vessels of less than 12 metres in length, instead of 10 metres in a Dutch EU Presidency compromise plan, will be exempted from the cutbacks after pressure from Sweden and other fishing countries.
